title: Fluctuation of lysine crotonylation confers azole tolerance in Candida auris
projectDescription: Candida auris, a human fungal pathogen, is a tremendous threat to the human community, causing recent fungal epidemics in over 40 countries with no effective antifungal treatment due to its rapidly developing drug tolerance. Recent studies identified several genomic mutations of drug targets1-3, 8, but only revealed a partial mechanism for drug tolerance in C. auris. Nevertheless, we found substantial tolerance of clinical C. auris isolates, which lack mutations in drug-tolerant genes, elicited by protein posttranslational modification strategies; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we map extensively five types of lysine (K) PTMs in C. auris under fluconazole (FLC) treatment conditions. Intriguingly, the FLC-resistant strain displayed a drug-responsive fluctuation for crotonylation, a key regulator for the oxidative phosphorylation pathway. The activation of crotonylation in FLC-resistant C. auris isolates confers drug-susceptible growth through the mitochondrial modulation of increases reactive oxygen species production, and repressed FLC tolerance-related genes. In addition, we demonstrate that this process of drug tolerance is horizontally conserved in prominent human fungal infections, such as Candida albicans and Cryptococcus neoformans. This study identifies a unique epiregulation of PTM that regulates drug tolerance, which may have consequences for antimicrobial drug tolerance and crotonylation in fungi and other eukaryotes.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The inhibition rate was determined using broth microdilution assay as described previously24, 25. Briefly, overnight cultures were washed twice with sterile PBS, which were added and incubated to 96-well plates containing antifungal drugs at 37 °C. The initial OD600 equals to 0.0025 and the growth was estimated 24h post incubation using MultiskanGO microplate reader (Thermo). Dose response data was quantitatively displayed with color using the program Java TreeView3. The 50% inhibitory concentration  (IC50) values were determined by performing nonlinear regression with GraphPad Prism Software version 8.32627. Candida auris strains, harvested from overnight cultures, were washed, diluted and sub-cultured in fresh YPD media with antifungal drugs. Fungal cells in the exponential phase were used. Proteins were isolated using a Mini-BeadBeater-16 (BioSpec) in HEPES buffer (50 mM HEPES, 140 mM NaCl, 1% Tritone X-100, 1 mM EDTA) supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktail (CWBIO) and 40 mM PMSF. Protein concentrations were quantified using the BCA assay.Immunoblotting was performed using the standard protocol as previously described28 and antibodies used in this study were as follows: Anti-Kac (1:2000, PTM Bio), Anti-Kub (1:2000 dilution, PTM Bio), Anti-Ksc (1:2000 dilution, PTM Bio), Anti-Kma (1:2000 dilution, PTM Bio), Anti-Kcr (1:2000 dilution, PTM Bio) and Anti-mouse and Anti-rabbit Secondary antibodies (1:5000 dilution, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The signal was captured using a ChemiDoc XRS+ (Bio-Rad). Overnight cultures of Candida auris strains were diluted in fresh YPD media and incubated at 37°C with antifungal drugs for about 6 h. Fungi cells were collected and frozen in liquid nitrogen and then stored in -80 °C. Comparative measurements of PTMs in Candida auris were performed in biological triplicates.   Acetylome, ubiquitome, malonylome, succinylome and crotonylome were performed at PTM Biolab Hangzhou (PTM Bio, China). Equal amounts of each sample protein were taken for enzymatic digestion and the volume was adjusted to the same with lysate solution. The precipitate was slowly added to a final concentration of 20% TCA, vortexed and mixed, and precipitated at 4°C for 2 h. The precipitate was centrifuged at 4500 g for 5 min and the precipitate was washed 2-3 times with pre-cooled acetone. After drying, 200 mM TEAB was added in the precipitate and the precipitate was sonicated to break up. Add trypsin at a ratio of 1:50 (protease: protein, m/m) and digest overnight. Dithiothreitol (DTT) was added to a final concentration of 5 mM and reduced for 30 min at 56°C. Iodoacetamide (IAA) was then added to a final concentration of 11 mM and incubated for 15 min at room temperature and protected from light.  The peptides were dissolved in IP buffer solution (100 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 50 mM Tris-HCl, 0.5% NP-40, pH 8.0). The supernatant was transferred to acetylation resin (PTM-104, PTM Bio) and incubated overnight on a shaker at 4 °C. After incubation, the resin was washed four times with IP buffer solution and twice with deionized water. The peptides bound to the resin were eluted with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid, and the eluate was collected and vacuum freeze dried. After drying, it was desalted according to the C18 ZipTips instructions and vacuum freeze dried for LC-MS analysis.  The peptides were separated using a High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC, NanoElute) system. Mobile phase A was a 0.1% formic acid and 2% acetonitrile aqueous solution, while mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid and 100% acetonitrile aqueous solution. After being dissolved in liquid chromatography mobile phase A, the peptides were separated. The liquid phase gradient was established as follows: 0-42 min, 7%-24% B; 42-54 min, 24%-32% B; 54-57 min, 32%-80% B; 57-60 min, 80% B, and flow rate maintained at 450nL/min. The peptides were separated using a UHPLC system and then injected into a Capillary ion source for ionization before being analyzed using a timsTOF Pro mass spectrometry system. The ion source voltage was set to 1.6 kV and both the peptide parent ion, and its secondary fragments were detected and analyzed using a high-resolution TOF. The secondary mass spectrometry scan range was set to 400-1500 m/z. The data acquisition mode was used in parallel accumulated serial fragmentation (PASEF) mode. A primary mass spectrum was acquired followed by 10 PASEF mode acquisitions of secondary spectra with parent ion charge numbers in the range 0-5. The dynamic exclusion time for the serial mass spectrometry scans was set to 30 s seconds to avoid duplication of parent ion scans.
dataProcessingProtocol: The resulting MS/MS data were processed using the MaxQuant search engine (v1.6.6.0) for this experiment29. The search parameters were set as follows: The database is Candida_auris_498019_PR_20201024.fasta (5409 sequences), an inverse library has been added to calculate the false positive rate (FDR) due to random matches, and a common contamination library has been added to the database to remove the effect of contaminating proteins from the identification results; Trypsin/P was used as the digestion method, and up to four missing cleavages were allowed; The minimum peptide length was set to 7 amino acid residues, while the maximum number of peptide modifications was set to 5; the mass error tolerance for the primary parent ion was set to 20 ppm for First search and 20 ppm for Main search, and the mass error tolerance for the secondary fragment ion was set to 20 ppm.   Carbamidomethyl (C) was set as a fixed modification and the variable modifications were oxidation of methionine, acetylation of the N-terminal of the protein and acetylation of lysine. The FDR for protein identification and PSM identification were set to 1%. To obtain high quality analysis results, further data filtering was required for the analysis. The FDR for the accuracy of identification at the spectral, peptide and protein levels is set at 1%; identified proteins need to contain at least one specific (unique) peptide.
